{{nihongo|'''Hitsujisaki Shrine'''|零羊崎神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Mutsu Province]].

'''Reiyōsaki Shrine''' (れいようさきじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} located in Mano, {{ill|Ishinomaki|Q270814|qid=Q270814}}, {{ill|Miyagi Prefecture|Q47896|qid=Q47896}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}) {{ill|Shikinai Ronsha|Q135022904|qid=Q135022904}}, and under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=former shrine ranking system}} it was classified as a {{ill|Son-sha|ja|村社|qid=Q134917284}}.

=== Enshrined deities ===
The enshrined deities are the following three (according to the stone pillar at the approach):
* '''{{ill|Toyotama-hime|lt=Toyotama-hime|Q2329261|qid=Q2329261|qid=Q2329261|lt=Toyotama-hime no Mikoto}}'''
* '''Akitsuhiko no Mikoto'''
* '''{{ill|Hayakitsuhiko and Hayakitsuhime|Q11326733|qid=Q11326733|lt=Hayakitsuhime no Mikoto}}'''

However, some sources, such as *Heisei Junpaiki Engishiki Inland Mutsu One Hundred Shrines*, introduce Toyotama-hime no Mikoto and {{ill|Ukanomitama|de|Ukanomitama|eo|Ukanomitama|fr|Uka-no-Mitama|ja|ウカノミタマ|mni|ꯎꯀꯅꯣꯃꯤꯇꯃ|ru|Ука-но митама|simple|Ukanomitama|sv|Ukanomitama|th|อูกาโนมิตามะ|zh|宇迦之御魂神|qid=Q3080728|lt=Ukanomitama no Mikoto}} as the enshrined deities.

=== History ===
=== Founding ===
The date of founding is unknown. *Fūnai Fudoki, Volume 13* ({{ill|1772|Q7690|qid=Q7690}}, {{ill|An'ei|Q1193910|qid=Q1193910}} 1)<ref>Included in *Fūnai Fudoki, Vol. 2* (1975).</ref> states that it is unclear when the shrine was enshrined.

=== Debate over identification as a Myōjin Taisha ===
During the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}, this shrine came to be identified with the Myōjin Taisha “Reiyōsaki Shrine.” “Reiyōsaki Shrine” appears in the *{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981}}* under the entry for the 27th day of the 1st month of {{ill|Jōgan|Q1075635|qid=Q1075635|lt=Jōgan}} 1 ({{ill|859|Q23897|qid=Q23897}}), as one of the 267 shrines granted promotion in {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|Q11591025|qid=Q11591025}}, having been elevated to {{ill|Junior Fourth Rank|Q11071127|qid=Q11071127}}<ref>In the entry for the 27th day of the 1st month of Jōgan 1 (859), the *Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku* reads: “Shōgoi no ge, kun yon-tō Shiha-hiko no kami. Kun go-tō Haibei Shi no kami. Kun roku-tō Reiyōsaki no kami. Jugo-i no jō, kun yon-tō Shiha-hime no kami, all Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade.” Thus, it is thought that prior to promotion the rank may have been Shōgoi no ge, kun roku-tō, though it is also possible that it was promoted from an unranked kun roku-tō.</ref>. In addition, in the *{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932}}* of {{ill|927|ab|927|af|927|am|927 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|927|ar|927|ary|927|ast|927|avk|927|az|927|azb|۹۲۷ (میلادی)|bar|927|bcl|927|be|927|be_x_old|927|bg|927|bn|৯২৭|bpy|মারি ৯২৭|br|927|bs|927.|ca|927|cdo|927 nièng|ceb|927|ckb|٩٢٧|crh|927|cs|927|csb|927|cv|927|cy|927|da|927|de|927|el|927|eml|927|eo|927|es|927|et|927|eu|927|fa|۹۲۷ (میلادی)|fi|927|fo|927|fr|927|fy|927|ga|927|gan|927年|gd|927|gl|927|he|927|hi|927|hr|927.|ht|927 (almanak jilyen)|hu|927|hy|927|id|927|ilo|927|io|927|is|927|it|927|ja|927年|jv|927|ka|927|kaa|927|kk|927 жыл|ko|927년|la|927|lb|927|lij|927|lmo|927|lt|927 m.|lv|927. gads|map_bms|927|mdf|927|mg|927|mhr|927|mi|927|mk|927|mr|इ.स. ९२७|mrj|927 и|ms|927|mzn|۹۲۷|nah|927|nap|927|nds|927|new|सन् ९२७|nl|927|nn|927|no|927|nrm|927|nso|927|oc|927|or|୯୨୭|os|927-æм аз|pl|927|pnb|927|pt|927|qu|927|ro|927|ru|927 год|rue|927|sa|९२७|scn|927|sd|927ع|se|927|sh|927.|shn|927|si|927|sk|927|smn|927|sq|927|sr|927|su|927|sv|927|sw|927|tg|Соли 927|th|พ.ศ. 1470|tk|927|tl|927|tly|927|tr|927|tt|927 ел|uk|927|ur|927ء|uz|927|vec|927|vi|927|war|927|wuu|927年|xmf|927|zh|927年|zh_min_nan|927 nî|zh_yue|927年|qid=Q30470}} ({{ill|Enchō|de|Enchō|fa|انچو|fr|Ère Enchō|ia|Encho|id|Enchō|ja|延長 (元号)|ko|엔초|ru|Энтё|simple|Enchō|sr|Енчо|tr|Enchō|uk|Ентьо|zh|延長 (日本)|zh_yue|延長 (年號)|qid=Q1327274|lt=Enchō}} 5), it is listed as a {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}, and in *{{ill|Engishiki|ar|إنجيشيكي (كتاب ياباني)|de|Engishiki|es|Engishiki|fr|Engishiki|he|אנגישיקי|id|Engishiki|it|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|ko|엔기시키|min|Engishiki|mr|इंगिशिकी|nl|Engishiki|pt|Engishiki|ru|Энгисики|simple|Engishiki|tr|Engishiki|uk|Енґісікі|zh|延喜式|qid=Q1342448}}*, Volume 3, it is recorded as a shrine subject to Myōjin rituals. However, the name Reiyōsaki Shrine disappears from later historical sources, and disputes arose during the Edo period.

In *Ōu Kankisekirōshi* written in {{ill|1719|Q6902|qid=Q6902}} ({{ill|Kyōhō|de|Kyōhō|es|Kyōhō|fa|کیوهو|fr|Ère Kyōhō|ja|享保|ko|교호|ru|Кёхо|simple|Kyōhō|sr|Кјохо|sv|Kyōhō|tr|Kyōhō|zh|享保|qid=Q1145048}} 4)<ref>Included in *Sendai Sōsho, Vol. 15: Ōu Kankisekirōshi (Upper)* (1972).</ref> and *Fūnai Meisekishi* written in {{ill|1741|Q7573|qid=Q7573}} ({{ill|Kanpō|Q1145798|qid=Q1145798}} 1)<ref>Included in *Sendai Sōsho, Vol. 8* (1972).</ref>, there is no mention of this shrine. However, in *Fūnai Fudoki, Volume 13* written in An’ei 1 (1772), the shrine is mentioned in the entry for Mano Village.

According to that account, as noted above, it was not clear when the shrine was enshrined; it was called Shiratori Shrine and was said to be the tutelary shrine of Mano Village, and local people said it was the ancient Reiyōsaki Shrine. As for the reason it was considered Reiyōsaki Shrine, the account states that Reiyōsaki Shrine was originally located at Makiyama in Minato Village, but after a fire it was relocated to Maruyama in Mano Village, where the {{ill|Kasai clan|Q6373969|qid=Q6373969}} had sacred fields. Therefore, markets were held before and after festivals and villagers gathered. As a result, the place where markets were held came to be called Miyakōji, and the place where the sacred fields had been came to be called Miyata; these remains still exist today. Moreover, because the shrine grounds face the direction of {{ill|wèi|Q20128396|qid=Q20128396}} (the “hitsuji” direction), villagers considered this shrine to be Reiyōsaki Shrine.

However, *Fūnai Fudoki, Volume 13* continues by stating that this theory is in fact not correct: at the end of the {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|Q1145058|qid=Q1145058}}, when the Kasai clan lost its territory and perished, Reiyōsaki Shrine also fell into ruin, and the mikoshi was moved to the Makiyama Kannon Hall in Minato Village. This mikoshi is no longer seen, and the divine name of Reiyōsaki Shrine was changed to Hakusan Shrine. It concludes by stating that these events were due to the machinations of Buddhist monks and are truly lamentable.

The entry for Minato Village in *Fūnai Fudoki, Volume 13* also describes the Reiyōsaki Shrine of Minato Village. According to it, the Reiyōsaki Shrine of Minato Village is currently called Hakusan Shrine and enshrines Toyotama-hiko no Mikoto; it was the foremost {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} in Oshika District and was in ancient times a grand shrine; and it serves as the tutelary shrine of the Seven Villages of Minato. Furthermore, in the description of Makiyama Daibikaku (Kannon Hall), it states that the site was the location of the ancient Reiyōsaki Shrine, which Buddhist monks seized, concealing the name Reiyōsaki Shrine and calling it Makiyama Kannon.

*Inai Town History* records that there was a dispute between the Reiyōsaki Shrine of Minato Village and this shrine. According to it, when the yamabushi ({{ill|Yamabushi|Q2309838|qid=Q2309838}}) of Fumyōin claimed that the Hakusan Shrine at Makiyama was Reiyōsaki Shrine, Kanshuin of Mano Village strongly protested, and the dispute was brought before the domain authorities. By summons dated the 26th day of the 2nd month of {{ill|1768|Q7675|qid=Q7675}} ({{ill|Meiwa|Q1146161|qid=Q1146161}} 5), the monk of Kanshuin appeared before the Sendai Magistrate’s Office on March 3 and was questioned about the matter of Reiyōsaki Shrine and the relationship between Fumyōin, Makiyama Hakusan Shrine, and Mano Reiyōsaki Shrine. Kanshuin responded that because Mano Village had suffered successive years of poor harvests and found it difficult to repair the shrine buildings, the mikoshi that had long been kept was temporarily entrusted to Makiyama Hakusan Shrine, and therefore the mikoshi did not originally belong to Makiyama. The Magistrate’s Office accepted this, ruled that Reiyōsaki Shrine should be worshiped as the tutelary shrine of Mano Village, and thus Kanshuin’s claim was successfully upheld<ref>From *Inai Town History, Part 9: Religion, Chapter 1: Shrines and Halls*. *Inai Town History* (1960).</ref>.

=== After the Meiji period ===
After the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ca|Shinbutsu bunri|de|Shinbutsu-Bunri|es|Shinbutsu bunri|fa|شینبوتسو بونری|fi|Shinbutsu bunri|fr|Shinbutsu bunri|id|Shinbutsu bunri|it|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離|ru|Симбуцу бунри|tr|Şinbutsu-bunri|zh|神佛分離|qid=Q1970535}} of the {{ill|Meiji era|ar|فترة مييجي|ast|Dómina Meiji|az|Meydzi dövrü|azb|مئی‌جی دؤورو|be|Перыяд Мэйдзі|bn|মেইজি যুগ|bo|མེའི་ཇིའི་དུས་དུས་མཚམས།|ca|Era Meiji|cs|Období Meidži|da|Meiji-perioden|de|Meiji-Zeit|el|Μεϊτζί (περίοδος)|es|Era Meiji|et|Meiji periood|eu|Meiji Aroa|fa|دوره میجی|fi|Meiji-kausi|fr|Ère Meiji|gl|Período Meiji|he|תקופת מייג'י|hr|Meiji (razdoblje)|ht|Epòk Meiji|hu|Meidzsi-kor|id|Zaman Meiji|io|Ero Meiji|is|Meiji-tímabilið|it|Periodo Meiji|ja|明治|ka|მეიძის ეპოქა|kbp|Mejii wɛɛ yaa alɩwaatʊ|kk|Мэйдзи дәуірі|ko|메이지 시대|la|Aetas Meiji|lt|Meidži laikotarpis|lv|Meidzi periods|mk|Меиџи (период)|mn|Мэйжийн эрин|ms|Zaman Meiji|nl|Meijiperiode|nn|Meiji|no|Meiji-perioden|pl|Meiji (okres)|pt|Era Meiji|ro|Perioada Meiji|ru|Мэйдзи|simple|Meiji period|sk|Obdobie Meidži|sq|Periudha Meixhi|sr|Меиџи период|sv|Meijiperioden|ta|மெய்சி காலம்|th|ยุคเมจิ|tl|Panahong Meiji|tr|Meiji Dönemi|uk|Період Мейдзі|ur|میجی دور|vi|Thời kỳ Minh Trị|war|Panahon Meiji|wuu|明治|zh|明治|zh_classical|明治|zh_min_nan|Bêng-tī|zh_yue|明治|qid=Q3125096}}, the shrine came to be called “Reiyōsaki Shrine.” In {{ill|1874|Q7761|qid=Q7761}} (Meiji 7), under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, it was listed as a village shrine and later designated a shrine receiving offerings of ritual food and heihaku. In Meiji 20 ({{ill|1887|Q7826|qid=Q7826}}), the shrine buildings were lost to fire, and at the time it was designated as a shrine receiving offerings, it was housed in a temporary shrine. The present shrine buildings were constructed thereafter.
